paper_metadata.title: Approximate complex amplitude encoding algorithm and its application to data classification problems

summary: The paper introduces Approximate Complex Amplitude Encoding (ACAE), a variational method for loading complex-valued data into quantum states using shallow circuits and classical-shadow fidelity estimation. Numerical demonstrations use a 5‑qubit, 12‑layer PQC achieving fidelity ≈0.994 for training-state preparation and >0.999 for test-state encoding, enabling a compact Hadamard classifier that correctly classifies 8/8 Iris setosa–versicolor samples and 8/8 selected credit-card fraud test samples (42/48 in a random test).

experiments.description: Approximate complex amplitude encoding (ACAE) training for complex-valued state preparation using a hardware-efficient parametrized quantum circuit and classical-shadow fidelity estimation.

algorithm.variant: Approximate complex amplitude encoding (ACAE) with fidelity-based training and classical shadows
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient ansatz with single-qubit Rx/Ry/Rz rotations and CNOT entanglers
algorithm.convergence_criteria: fixed 400 training iterations for the training-data encoder; fixed 100 iterations for the test-data encoder

hyperparameters.learning_rate_schedule: 0.1 for first 100 iterations, 0.01 for next 100, 0.005 for next 100, 0.001 for last 100
hyperparameters.random_initialization: randomly initialize all rotation axes (X/Y/Z) and angles
hyperparameters.fidelity_target: maximize fidelity between model state and target state

algorithm.parameter_initialization: random initialization of rotation axes and angles

problem_formulation.encoding_details: encode a complex-valued data vector into amplitudes of an n-qubit state; for the classifier, training data are embedded into the real and imaginary parts of amplitudes for the ancilla-0 branch and test data into the ancilla-1 branch
problem_formulation.objective_function: maximize fidelity f(θ)=|<Data|ψ(θ)>|^2 between target state and model state

problem_instance.description: Complex-valued data loading for classification; demonstrated on Iris binary classification and credit card fraud detection
problem_instance.dataset_name: Iris dataset; Kaggle credit card fraud dataset

dataset_specification.description: Iris: use first four samples of I. setosa and I. versicolor for training, and IDs 5-8 and 55-58 for testing; fraud: use 4 normal and 4 fraudulent transactions for training, and top four remaining normal/fraudulent IDs for testing

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Iris and fraud datasets are reduced to 4 features; fraud dataset uses PCA-transformed features V1-V4 from the Kaggle creditcardfraud dataset
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: numerical simulation / proof-of-principle classification; classification accuracy reported on selected test instances

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; classical shadow estimation; parameter-shift gradients
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: normalize data vectors; select subsets of Iris and credit-card datasets; use PCA features for fraud dataset
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: measure ancilla Z expectation and take sign for class label

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: fidelity increases during training; final fidelity reported as 0.994 for Iris training encoder and >0.999 for test encoders

speedup_claims.factor: O(poly(n)) gate depth vs O(2^n) exact state preparation
speedup_claims.baseline_method: exact amplitude encoding / exact state preparation
speedup_claims.conditions: for preparing general complex-valued data vectors on a quantum circuit
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not prove an end-to-end algorithmic speedup; the advantage is reduced circuit depth for approximate state preparation, while classical fidelity evaluation still scales exponentially in the number of amplitudes.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: ACAE state preparation uses O(poly(n)) gates for the PQC; classical-shadow fidelity estimation uses random Clifford sampling
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: exact state preparation requires O(2^n) CNOT gates; classical evaluation of fidelity estimate involves O(2^n) summation over amplitudes

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: unknown; authors only argue that ACAE reduces state preparation depth from O(2^n) to O(poly(n)) using a variational circuit
limiting_factors: exponential classical computation during fidelity evaluation
barren plateau risk with fidelity cost
superlinear circuit depth scaling observed in simulations
random Clifford measurements required for classical shadow estimation

notes: The paper presents numerical experiments and circuit constructions, but does not name a specific hardware device or QPU; hardware.type is therefore not specified.

The 5-qubit, 12-layer ansatz is explicitly reported for the Iris training encoder; the 2-qubit, 2-layer ansatz is reported for the test-data encoder, but the main experiment is summarized here as the ACAE/CHC workflow with the training encoder resources.
No transpiled depth, gate counts, or QPU calibration data are reported.
The paper does not claim demonstrated quantum advantage; it proposes a method for approximate amplitude encoding using shallow circuits.

experiments.description: ACAE-based compact Hadamard classifier applied to Iris setosa vs Iris versicolor binary classification.

algorithm.variant: Compact Hadamard classifier implemented with ACAE-encoded training and test states
algorithm.ansatz: training encoder: 5-qubit, 12-layer hardware-efficient ansatz; test encoder: 2-qubit, 2-layer Ry+CNOT ansatz
algorithm.convergence_criteria: fixed 400 iterations for training encoder; fixed 100 iterations for each test encoder
algorithm.parameter_initialization: random initialization of rotation axes and angles

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Iris feature vectors are embedded as complex amplitudes; training data occupy real and imaginary parts of the ancilla-0 branch, test data are encoded in the ancilla-1 branch
problem_formulation.objective_function: binary classification via sign of <σ_z^(A)> = sign[1/2 Σ_j b'_j y_j <x~|x_j>]
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: uniform weights b_j=2/M; phase ϕ chosen as π/4 for balanced classes

problem_instance.description: Binary classification of Iris setosa vs Iris versicolor

dataset_specification.description: Training: IDs 1-4 (I. setosa) and 51-54 (I. versicolor); Testing: IDs 5-8 and 55-58

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Use four features: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width; normalize amplitudes to satisfy state normalization
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 8 held-out test instances; classification correctness reported per instance

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; classical-shadow fidelity estimation; parameter-shift gradients
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: select Iris samples; normalize feature vectors; train encoder off-line on training data; train separate test encoder per test datum
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: measure ancilla qubit in computational basis and classify by sign of expectation value

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: fidelity rises to 0.994 for training encoder; test encoders exceed 0.999

speedup_claims.factor: compact classifier with O(poly(n)) approximate encoding instead of exponential exact encoding
speedup_claims.baseline_method: original compact Hadamard classifier requiring exact compact amplitude encoding
speedup_claims.conditions: for Iris binary classification using ACAE-encoded training and test states
speedup_claims.caveats: No classical classifier baseline is reported; the paper reports only correctness on held-out test instances and compares against exact-data encoding qualitatively.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(n)) gate-depth state preparation via ACAE; CHC evaluation via ancilla measurement
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: exact compact amplitude encoding and uniformly controlled gates require exponential resources in the number of qubits

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: would require scalable amplitude encoding for large datasets; current experiment uses only 5 qubits and 8 training samples
limiting_factors: no runtime or resource comparison demonstrating advantage

notes: The paper reports the 5-qubit, 12-layer training encoder and 2-qubit, 2-layer test encoder; the experiment is summarized with the training encoder resources because the classifier workflow uses both.
No actual QPU or simulator backend is named; this is a numerical proof-of-principle experiment.
The Iris experiment is presented as a proof-of-principle demonstration of the encoding and classifier, not as a performance comparison with classical ML.

experiments.description: ACAE-based compact Hadamard classifier applied to credit card fraud detection using Kaggle creditcardfraud data.

algorithm.variant: Compact Hadamard classifier implemented with ACAE-encoded training and test states
algorithm.ansatz: training encoder: 5-qubit, 12-layer hardware-efficient ansatz; test encoder: 2-qubit, 2-layer Ry+CNOT ansatz
algorithm.convergence_criteria: fixed 400 iterations for training encoder; fixed 100 iterations for each test encoder
algorithm.parameter_initialization: random initialization of rotation axes and angles

problem_formulation.encoding_details: encode 4 selected PCA features of each transaction into complex amplitudes; normal transactions and fraudulent transactions are mapped to the real and imaginary parts of the ancilla-0 branch, respectively
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: uniform weights; phase ϕ chosen to balance classes

problem_instance.description: Binary classification of normal vs fraudulent credit card transactions

dataset_specification.description: Training: 4 normal and 4 fraudulent transactions; Testing: top four remaining normal IDs and top four remaining fraudulent IDs, excluding training data

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Use PCA-transformed features V1-V4 from the Kaggle creditcardfraud dataset; normalize amplitudes
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 8 held-out test instances; classification correctness reported per instance; additional simulation on 48 randomly selected instances with 42 correct classifications

implementation_details.classical_solver: Adam optimizer; classical-shadow fidelity estimation; parameter-shift gradients
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: select 4 normal and 4 fraudulent training samples; use PCA features V1-V4; normalize feature vectors
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: measure ancilla qubit and classify by sign of expectation value

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: training fidelity reaches 0.994; test encoders exceed 0.999; 42/48 correct on additional random-instance simulation

speedup_claims.factor: compact classifier with O(poly(n)) approximate encoding instead of exponential exact encoding
speedup_claims.baseline_method: original compact Hadamard classifier requiring exact compact amplitude encoding
speedup_claims.conditions: for credit card fraud detection using ACAE-encoded training and test states
speedup_claims.caveats: No classical fraud-detection baseline is reported. The paper reports an additional simulation on 48 randomly selected instances with 42 correct classifications, but does not compare against a classical model.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(n)) gate-depth state preparation via ACAE; CHC evaluation via ancilla measurement
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: exact compact amplitude encoding and uniformly controlled gates require exponential resources in the number of qubits

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: authors estimate that handling the full dataset (≈280k transactions with 28 features) would require ~23 qubits
limiting_factors: training dataset reduced to only 8 samples
variational training and classical shadow overhead

notes: The paper reports the same ACAE/CHC circuit resources as in the Iris experiment; the fraud-detection task differs only in dataset and selected features.
No hardware backend is specified; results are from numerical simulation/proof-of-concept evaluation.
The fraud detection example is a proof-of-concept classification experiment using extremely small training sets.

experiments.description: Scalability simulation evaluating how circuit depth required for ACAE grows with the number of qubits (data size).

algorithm.optimizer: Adam (same training procedure as main experiments)

key_results: Simulation varying problem size from 64 to 1024 data elements (5 to 9 qubits).
Measured circuit depth required to reach fidelity thresholds of 0.90, 0.95, and 0.99.
Required circuit depth grows superlinearly with qubit count.
For the largest tested case (1024 data points, 9 qubits), only the fidelity ≥0.90 depth could be computed due to classical resource limits.
